name: Dollar bid-offer spread
prompt: What is the dollar bid-offer spread of an asset, from its quoted prices?

variables.meaning: dollar bid-offer spread
the higher quote: the price at which a trader sells to you
the lower quote: the price at which a trader buys from you

corruptions.why: The offer is the higher quote, so this gives a negative spread.
That is the half-spread you pay on one side of the mid, not the spread itself.

sensitivities.why: A higher offer with the bid fixed widens the spread.
A higher bid with the offer fixed narrows the spread.

intuition: The spread is the round-trip toll the dealer charges: buy at the high quote, sell at the low one.

name: Proportional bid-offer spread
prompt: How do you express the bid-offer spread as a pure number, relative to the fair price of the asset?

variables.meaning: proportional bid-offer spread, a pure number (decimal)
the higher quote: the price at which a trader sells to you
the lower quote: the price at which a trader buys from you
price halfway between bid and offer; regarded as the fair price

corruptions.why: The spread is scaled by the mid-market (fair) price, not by the offer.
The halving belongs in the liquidation cost (s times alpha over 2), not in the definition of s.

sensitivities.why: A higher offer with bid and mid fixed widens the spread.
A higher bid with offer and mid fixed narrows the spread.
The same dollar spread is a smaller fraction of a pricier asset.

intuition: Put the dollar spread on a per-dollar basis so you can compare a $90 share with a $15 commodity.

name: Cost of liquidation in a normal market
prompt: What does it cost to liquidate a book of n positions in normal market conditions, from each position's value and its normal proportional spread?

variables.meaning: dollar cost of unwinding the whole book at normal spreads, prices unchanged
estimated proportional bid-offer spread of instrument i in normal conditions (decimal: dollar spread / mid-market price)
dollar (mid-market) value of the position in instrument i
number of positions (instruments) in the book

corruptions.why: Drops the halving: a sale happens at the bid, only half the spread away from the mid.
Spreads widen together, so the costs are simply added; there is no diversification across instruments.
The cost scales up with position size, it does not fall as the position grows.

sensitivities.why: A wider spread means a bigger haircut on every dollar sold.
A bigger position pays half the spread on more dollars.

intuition: Each position pays half its spread on every dollar: you cross from the mid to one side only.

name: Cost of liquidation in a stressed market
prompt: What is the worst-case (confidence-level) cost of liquidating a book, given the mean and volatility of each instrument's proportional spread?

variables.meaning: dollar cost of unwinding the book that will not be exceeded at the chosen confidence level, prices unchanged
mean of the proportional bid-offer spread of instrument i (decimal, not dollars)
confidence parameter for the spread distribution (e.g. 2.326 for a 99% worst case with normal spreads)
standard deviation of the proportional bid-offer spread of instrument i (decimal, not dollars)
dollar (mid-market) value of the position in instrument i
number of positions (instruments) in the book

corruptions.why: Stress widens the spread: the worst case is above the mean spread, not below it.
Omits lambda, so the spread is only one standard deviation wide and ignores the confidence level.
Lambda multiplies the standard deviation of the spread, not its variance.

sensitivities.why: A wider average spread raises the stressed spread one-for-one.
More volatile spreads blow out further at the confidence level.
A higher confidence level pushes further into the spread's tail.
A bigger position pays the stressed half-spread on more dollars.

intuition: Same half-spread cost, but the spread is stretched to its bad-day width: mean plus lambda standard deviations.

name: Liquidity-adjusted VaR (normal market)
prompt: How do you adjust a book's VaR for the cost of unwinding it at normal bid-offer spreads?

variables.meaning: liquidity-adjusted VaR using normal spreads
regular value at risk of the book (worst-case mark-to-market change)
estimated proportional bid-offer spread of instrument i in normal conditions (decimal: dollar spread / mid-market price)
dollar (mid-market) value of the position in instrument i
number of positions (instruments) in the book

corruptions.why: LVaR adds the two terms outright; there is no diversification between price risk and liquidation cost.
The liquidation cost is an extra loss, so it increases the risk measure.
The two are added, never averaged.

sensitivities.why: LVaR rises one-for-one with VaR.
Wider spreads raise the liquidation cost added on top.
Bigger positions cost more to unwind.

intuition: Price risk plus exit cost: what you can lose from the market moving, plus what you pay to get out.

name: Liquidity-adjusted VaR (stressed market)
prompt: How do you adjust a book's VaR for the worst-case cost of unwinding it when spreads are stressed?

variables.meaning: liquidity-adjusted VaR using stressed spreads
regular value at risk of the book (worst-case mark-to-market change)
mean of the proportional bid-offer spread of instrument i (decimal, not dollars)
confidence parameter for the spread distribution (e.g. 2.326 for a 99% worst case with normal spreads)
standard deviation of the proportional bid-offer spread of instrument i (decimal, not dollars)
dollar (mid-market) value of the position in instrument i
number of positions (instruments) in the book

corruptions.why: The addition is unconditional: no correlation adjustment between VaR and the liquidation cost.
The stressed spread is the mean plus lambda standard deviations, not minus.
That is the normal-market LVaR; the stressed version uses the mean-plus-lambda-sigma spread.

sensitivities.why: LVaR rises one-for-one with VaR.
A wider average spread raises the stressed liquidation cost.
More volatile spreads blow out further at the confidence level.
A higher spread confidence level widens the stressed spread.
Bigger positions cost more to unwind.

intuition: Bad-day price loss plus bad-day exit cost, stacked on top of each other.

name: Liquidity coverage ratio (LCR)
prompt: What Basel III ratio tests whether a bank can survive a 30-day acute stress, and what is its minimum?
latex: \text{LCR} = \frac{\text{High-quality liquid assets}}{\text{Net cash outflows in a 30-day period}} \geq 100\%

variables.meaning: Basel III liquidity coverage ratio (percent)
stock of high-quality liquid assets
net cash outflows over a 30-day period of acute stress (three-notch downgrade, deposit loss, wholesale funding loss, haircuts, credit-line drawdowns)

corruptions.latex: \text{LCR} = \frac{\text{Net cash outflows in a 30-day period}}{\text{High-quality liquid assets}} \geq 100\%
corruptions.why: Liquid assets must cover the outflows, so they sit in the numerator.

corruptions.latex: \text{LCR} = \frac{\text{High-quality liquid assets}}{\text{Net cash outflows in a 12-month period}} \geq 100\%
corruptions.why: The LCR horizon is a 30-day stress period, not a year.

corruptions.latex: \text{LCR} = \frac{\text{High-quality liquid assets}}{\text{Net cash outflows in a 30-day period}} \geq 60\%
corruptions.why: 60% was only the 2015 phase-in level; the full requirement (from 2019) is 100%.

sensitivities.why: More liquid assets cover the same outflows more comfortably.
Larger stressed outflows in the denominator mean the same liquid assets cover a smaller share of them.

intuition: Cash-like assets on hand must at least cover a month of stressed net outflows.

name: Net stable funding ratio (NSFR)
prompt: What Basel III ratio tests the long-term stability of a bank's funding against its assets, and what is its minimum?
latex: \text{NSFR} = \frac{\text{Amount of stable funding}}{\text{Required amount of stable funding}} \geq 100\%

variables.meaning: Basel III net stable funding ratio (percent)
each funding category (capital, wholesale deposits, retail deposits, ...) times its available stable funding (ASF) factor
assets and off-balance-sheet items needing funding, each times its required stable funding (RSF) factor

corruptions.latex: \text{NSFR} = \frac{\text{Required amount of stable funding}}{\text{Amount of stable funding}} \geq 100\%
corruptions.why: ASF-weighted funding is the numerator; RSF-weighted assets are the denominator.

corruptions.latex: \text{NSFR} = \frac{\text{High-quality liquid assets}}{\text{Required amount of stable funding}} \geq 100\%
corruptions.why: High-quality liquid assets are the LCR numerator; the NSFR numerator is ASF-weighted funding.

sensitivities.why: More stable (higher-ASF) funding raises the ratio.
More hard-to-liquidate (high-RSF) assets raise the denominator, so the same stable funding covers less.

intuition: Stable money in (liabilities weighted by ASF) must at least match the stable money the assets need (weighted by RSF).

name: GEV distribution, tail index not zero (Frechet/Weibull)
prompt: By the Fisher-Tippett theorem, what distribution function do sample maxima converge to when the tail index is non-zero?

variables.meaning: GEV cumulative probability that the extreme (sample maximum M_n) is no greater than x
the extreme value being evaluated
location parameter (related to, but not the same as, the mean)
scale parameter (related to, but not the same as, the standard deviation)
tail index: sets the shape (heaviness) of the tail; > 0 Frechet, = 0 Gumbel, < 0 Weibull

corruptions.why: The exponent is minus one over the tail index.
Without the leading minus inside the exp the value exceeds 1, so it cannot be a probability.
The standardisation divides by the scale parameter sigma, not by its square.

sensitivities.why: It is a cumulative distribution function, so it rises with x.
A higher location shifts the distribution right, leaving less probability below a given x.
Down if x is above mu (the standardised distance shrinks), up if x is below mu.
With x, mu and sigma fixed (x not equal to mu), a larger tail index enlarges the power term inside the exp on both sides of mu, so F falls: more probability is pushed into the upper tail.

intuition: Standardise x by location and scale, bend it through the tail index power, then double-negative-exponentiate: bigger xi, fatter tail.

name: GEV distribution, tail index zero (Gumbel)
prompt: What form does the GEV distribution take in the light-tailed case where the tail index equals zero?

variables.meaning: GEV cumulative probability that the extreme (sample maximum M_n) is no greater than x
the extreme value being evaluated
location parameter (related to, but not the same as, the mean)
scale parameter (related to, but not the same as, the standard deviation)
tail index; equal to 0 in this (Gumbel) case

corruptions.why: The Gumbel is a double exponential; this drops the inner exp.
Standardise by the scale parameter sigma, not by sigma squared.
That single-exponential shape is the GP (POT) distribution at xi = 0, not the Gumbel GEV.

intuition: Tail index zero: the power law of the Frechet collapses into an exponential inside an exponential, so the tail is light.

name: Distribution of excess losses over a threshold (POT)
prompt: In the peaks-over-threshold approach, how is the distribution of the excess over a high threshold u written in terms of the loss distribution F?
latex: F_u(x) = P\{X - u \le x \mid X > u\} = \frac{F(x+u) - F(u)}{1 - F(u)}

variables.meaning: distribution of the excess over the threshold, conditional on the threshold having been breached
the loss (random variable)
the chosen high threshold
size of the excess above the threshold
cumulative distribution function of the underlying losses

corruptions.latex: F_u(x) = P\{X - u \le x \mid X > u\} = \frac{F(x+u) - F(u)}{F(u)}
corruptions.why: Condition on exceeding u, whose probability is 1 - F(u), not F(u).

corruptions.latex: F_u(x) = P\{X - u \le x \mid X > u\} = F(x+u) - F(u)
corruptions.why: Without dividing by 1 - F(u) this is the unconditional probability, not the conditional excess distribution.

corruptions.latex: F_u(x) = P\{X - u \le x \mid X > u\} = \frac{F(x) - F(u)}{1 - F(u)}
corruptions.why: x is the excess measured from u, so the loss level is x + u, not x.

sensitivities.why: Raising F at x + u raises the result; raising F(u) with F(x + u) fixed lowers it.

intuition: Probability of landing between u and u + x, rescaled by the probability of getting past u at all.

name: Generalized Pareto distribution, tail index not zero
prompt: By the GPBdH theorem, what distribution does the excess-loss distribution converge to as the threshold rises, when the tail index is non-zero?

variables.meaning: tail (shape) index, the same as in GEV theory
excess loss over the threshold
scale parameter of the GP distribution

corruptions.why: The exponent is minus one over xi; with plus the bracket grows and the value goes negative.
The excess x is scaled by beta, so x is in the numerator.
The bracket is one plus xi x over beta.

sensitivities.why: It is a cumulative distribution, so it rises with the excess.
A larger scale spreads the excesses out, leaving less probability below a given x (for x > 0).
A larger tail index fattens the tail, so less probability sits below a given x (for x > 0).

intuition: One minus a power-law survival probability: the tail index sets how slowly big excesses die off.

name: Generalized Pareto distribution, tail index zero
prompt: What form does the generalized Pareto distribution of excess losses take when the tail index equals zero?

variables.meaning: excess loss over the threshold
scale parameter of the GP distribution

corruptions.why: The excess is scaled by beta, so x is the numerator.
That is the survival probability; the distribution function is one minus it.
Without the minus the exponential grows and the value goes negative.

sensitivities.why: It is a cumulative distribution, so it rises with the excess.
A larger scale spreads the excesses out, leaving less probability below a given x.

intuition: At xi = 0 the excesses are simply exponential with mean-like scale beta.

name: Put-call parity (present-value form)
prompt: What links the prices of a European call and put with the same strike and maturity to the spot price and the strike?

variables.meaning: European call price
European put price (same strike and maturity)
spot price of the underlying
present value of the strike price
strike price

corruptions.why: A call is worth more relative to the put when the spot is high, so S enters with a plus.
The strike is paid at maturity, so it must be discounted to present value.
Parity is about the difference between call and put, not their sum.

sensitivities.why: A higher spot raises the call relative to the put.
A higher (present value of the) strike favours the put over the call.

intuition: Long call plus short put is a synthetic forward: worth spot minus the discounted strike.

name: Put-call parity with dividend yield (continuous compounding)
prompt: Write put-call parity for a European option on an asset paying a continuous dividend yield, using continuously compounded discounting.
latex: p + S_0 e^{-qT} = c + K e^{-rT}

variables.meaning: European put price
spot price
dividend yield (decimal, continuous)
time to maturity (years)
European call price
strike price (also written X)
risk-free rate (decimal, continuous)

corruptions.latex: p + S_0 e^{-rT} = c + K e^{-qT}
corruptions.why: The spot is discounted at the dividend yield q; the strike at the risk-free rate r.
Drops the dividend adjustment: the spot must be reduced by e to the minus qT.

corruptions.latex: p + K e^{-rT} = c + S_0 e^{-qT}
corruptions.why: The put pairs with the (dividend-adjusted) spot, the call with the discounted strike.

sensitivities.why: With strike, rates and maturity fixed, a dearer call means the put side must be dearer too.
A higher strike raises the discounted strike on the call side, so the put side rises.
A higher rate shrinks the discounted strike, so the put side falls.

intuition: Protective put (put plus dividend-adjusted stock) equals fiduciary call (call plus discounted strike).

name: Market-minus-BSM pricing error is the same for puts and calls
prompt: Subtracting put-call parity at BSM prices from parity at market prices, how does the put's pricing error relate to the call's?

variables.meaning: market price of the European put
Black-Scholes-Merton price of the put
market price of the European call (same strike and maturity)
Black-Scholes-Merton price of the call

corruptions.why: The deviations have the same sign: if the call is dear to BSM, so is the put.
The PV(X) and S0 e^{-qt} terms cancel when the two parity equations are subtracted.

sensitivities.why: A dearer market call (BSM fixed) implies an equally dearer market put.
A higher BSM call value with market prices fixed shrinks the call's (and so the put's) deviation.

intuition: Same strike, same maturity: the market over- or under-prices the call and the put by the same dollars, so they share one implied volatility.

name: BSM delta versus minimum variance delta (equity skew)
prompt: With a negative relation between equity prices and implied volatility, how does the BSM delta compare with the minimum variance delta?

variables.meaning: Black-Scholes-Merton delta (assumes implied volatility unchanged when the price moves)
delta that accounts for the relationship between implied volatilities and equity prices

corruptions.why: When equity rises, implied vol falls and cuts the option value, so the minimum variance delta is the smaller one.
Equality would only hold if implied volatility did not move with the equity price, which is what the skew says it does.

intuition: Price up means vol down, which drags the option value back, so the true hedge ratio is below the BSM one.

name: Stressed liquid asset buffer (contingent liquidity)
prompt: How do you estimate the contingent liquidity left under a stress scenario, starting from the normal liquid asset buffer?
latex: \text{Stressed liquid asset buffer} = \text{Normal liquid asset buffer} - \text{Stressed cash outflows} + \text{Stressed cash inflows}

variables.meaning: contingent liquidity available under the stress scenario
starting stock of liquid investments, liquidity facility availability and unrestricted deposits
cash outflows under the stress scenario
cash inflows under the stress scenario

corruptions.latex: \text{Stressed liquid asset buffer} = \text{Normal liquid asset buffer} + \text{Stressed cash outflows} - \text{Stressed cash inflows}
corruptions.why: Outflows drain the buffer and inflows replenish it, not the reverse.

corruptions.latex: \text{Stressed liquid asset buffer} = \text{Normal liquid asset buffer} - \text{Stressed cash outflows} + \text{Normal cash inflows}
corruptions.why: Both legs must be stressed; using normal inflows against stressed outflows overstates the buffer.

corruptions.latex: \text{Stressed liquid asset buffer} = \text{Normal liquid asset buffer} - \text{Stressed cash outflows}
corruptions.why: Stressed inflows are added back after the outflows are taken out.

sensitivities.why: A bigger starting buffer leaves more after the stress.
Larger stressed outflows drain more of the buffer.
Larger stressed inflows put more back.

intuition: A waterfall: start with the normal buffer, take out stressed outflows, put back stressed inflows.
